name: Serbian Karađorđeva Šnicla
description: Karađorđeva šnicla has a real, specific origin - invented in 1956 by chef Milovan 'Mića' Stojanović, who received a surprise order for Chicken Kiev but lacked chicken or butter, and improvised with veal and sour cream instead; the guest turned out to be President Tito's daughter-in-law, and the dish became a national icon. Real presentation arranges lemon and red pepper specifically to reflect the colors of the Serbian national emblem, not just as garnish.

steps_detailed: Pound the chicken thin and even between plastic wrap.
Spread the sour cream generously in the center, then roll up tightly, tucking in the sides.
Dredge in the flour, then the egg, then the breadcrumbs, coating fully.
Fry in the oil, turning, 4-5 minutes per side, until deeply golden and cooked through.
Serve with the lemon and a dusting of paprika arranged together - real tradition intends these to echo the colors of the Serbian emblem.

name: Serbian Pljeskavica
description: Pljeskavica, a real grilled meat patty often called the Serbian burger, real technique kneads the meat well and lets it rest so it holds together on the grill without falling apart.
steps_detailed: Mix the beef with the onion, garlic, pepper, and salt, kneading by hand 5 minutes until cohesive.
Shape into a wide, flat patty and let rest 15 minutes.
Grill over medium-high heat, turning once, 5-6 minutes per side, until well charred and cooked through.

name: Serbian Ajvar
description: Ajvar, a roasted red pepper and eggplant relish, is one of Serbia's most essential condiments, real technique roasting both vegetables until the skins char fully for genuine smoky depth.
steps_detailed: Roast the bell pepper and eggplant at 450F (230C) for 25-30 minutes, turning once, until the skins are fully charred and blistered.
Let cool slightly, then peel off the skins.
Blend or mash with the garlic, olive oil, and vinegar.

name: Serbian Šopska Salata
description: Šopska salata, Serbia's real village salad, is genuinely built on ripe tomatoes and real grated cheese falling as a light, fluffy blanket over the top, real technique using a box grater rather than crumbling the cheese by hand.
steps_detailed: Toss the tomatoes, cucumber, bell pepper, and onion with the olive oil.
Grate the feta directly over the top, so it falls in light, fluffy shreds forming a real blanket over the vegetables.

name: Serbian Sarma
description: Sarma, cabbage rolls stuffed with rice and meat, are a genuine Serbian staple shared with the wider Balkans, real technique using well-softened, pliable cabbage leaves so they roll without tearing.
steps_detailed: Blanch the cabbage leaves 3-4 minutes until fully pliable.
Mix the raw rice with the beef and onion.
Roll a spoonful of the filling tightly into each cabbage leaf.
Arrange in a pot, cover with the tomatoes and enough water to just cover, and simmer 40-45 minutes until the rice is tender.

name: Serbian Grilled Fish
description: Grilled fish rubbed with garlic and lemon, reflecting Serbia's Danube and Sava River fishing tradition.
steps_detailed: Rub the fish with the garlic and lemon juice, and let sit 10 minutes.
Grill or broil, 4-5 minutes per side, until just cooked through.

name: Serbian Roasted Walnuts
description: A simple roasted walnut snack, common across Serbia.
steps_detailed: Toast the walnuts in a dry pan over medium heat, stirring often, 4-5 minutes, until fragrant.

name: Serbian Beef and Vegetable Stew
description: A simple, hearty beef and vegetable stew, common Serbian home cooking outside the specific named dishes.
steps_detailed: Brown the beef with the onion, 8-9 minutes.
Add the carrot, potato, and tomatoes, and simmer 30-35 minutes until tender.
